issues.legal_issue: The available methods for disposing of liquor licences are alternatives, and the licensing authority is not required to try them in a prescribed sequence.
material_facts: The rules listed disposal by tender, auction, fixed licence fee, or another manner directed by the State Government.
The State Government chose a method of disposal under its policy decision rather than first attempting tender, auction, and fixed licence fee.
issues.conclusion: The licensing authority may choose any one of the listed methods, provided that its application does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Rule XXII of the Madhya Pradesh Excise Rules treats the four disposal methods as alternatives; its language requires neither sequential resort to them nor reasons for choosing a later-listed method. The equality requirement under Article 14 of the Constitution applies regardless of the method chosen.

predicates.licence_disposal_case: The proceeding concerns the method used by a public authority to dispose of a licence.
predicates.rule_lists_alternative_methods: The governing rule lists several methods of disposal as available choices.

issues.definition: When a licence-disposal proceeding concerns a rule listing alternative methods, the authority may choose any listed method.

issues.legal_issue: A licence subject to an unamended maximum-term rule cannot be treated as renewable beyond that maximum so as to confer an indefinite monopoly.
material_facts: The governing rule limited wholesale licences to a maximum term of five years.
Although the policy materials contemplated renewal after an initial term, the relevant Act and rule were not amended.
The licence documents provided for renewal each year within the stated five-year term.
issues.conclusion: The licences were limited to a maximum period of five years and did not create an indefinite monopoly.
issues.legal_principle: Section 62(2)(h) of the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act authorized rules prescribing licence terms, and Rule II of the Rules of General Application imposed a maximum term of five years. An intention to provide for renewal beyond that limit could not take effect without the necessary amendment to the governing law or rules.

predicates.licence_term_case: The proceeding concerns the duration or renewal of a licence.
predicates.maximum_term_rule_unamended: The governing rule sets a maximum licence term and remains unamended.
predicates.renewal_operates_within_stated_term: The licence provides for renewal during its stated term rather than expressly extending beyond that term.

issues.definition: When a licence-term proceeding involves an unamended maximum-term rule and renewal within the stated term, the licence cannot create an indefinite monopoly.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not divide an integrated government policy and invalidate only part of it where doing so would create a new policy and disrupt accrued rights.
material_facts: The policy linked construction of new distilleries by existing contractors with the grant of licences to operate them and supply liquor.
The contractors had acquired land, built facilities, ordered equipment, and incurred substantial expenditure in reliance on the policy.
The High Court upheld the construction component but invalidated the licensing component.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in severing the integrated policy and invalidating only one component.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot make a new policy for the government by sustaining one inseparable part of a policy and striking down another. Where the components form one integrated arrangement, partial invalidation may create a different policy and cause hardship, injustice, and public inconvenience.

predicates.policy_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges a government policy.
predicates.policy_components_integrated: The challenged policy links its components as parts of one arrangement.
predicates.third_parties_substantially_rely_on_poli: Third parties take substantial steps and incur significant costs in reliance on the policy.
predicates.partial_invalidation_would_create_new_po: Invalidating only part of the arrangement would produce a policy different from the one the government adopted.

issues.definition: When a policy challenge concerns an integrated arrangement relied on by third parties, and partial invalidation would create a new policy, the court must not sever the arrangement.

issues.legal_issue: Unexplained, inordinate delay coupled with intervening third-party rights may justify refusing discretionary writ relief.
material_facts: The petitioners waited many months after the policy decision before filing their writ petitions, and the Court found that the delay was not adequately explained.
During the interval, the licence holders acquired land, constructed distillery buildings, purchased equipment, and spent substantial resources.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners were disentitled to relief in the exercise of the High Court's writ jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary. Unexplained delay, particularly when third-party rights have intervened, may lead a court to refuse relief because belated intervention can cause hardship, injustice, confusion, and public inconvenience. The rule is not rigid and may yield where the demands of justice compellingly require intervention. The Court relied on Ramanna Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India and Ashok Kumar Mishra v. Collector, Raipur.

rule.if: writ_petition_case and unexplained_inordinate_delay and third_party_rights_intervened and third_parties_substantially_rely_on_action

predicates.writ_petition_case: The proceeding seeks discretionary relief through a writ petition.
predicates.unexplained_inordinate_delay: The petitioner waits an inordinate time to bring the challenge and does not satisfactorily explain the delay.
predicates.third_party_rights_intervened: Rights or interests of third parties arise while the petitioner delays bringing the challenge.
predicates.third_parties_substantially_rely_on_acti: Third parties take substantial steps or incur significant costs in reliance on the challenged action.

issues.definition: When an unexplained, inordinate delay in a writ proceeding allows third-party rights and substantial reliance to arise, the court may refuse writ relief.

issues.legal_issue: The State remains subject to the equality guarantee when it grants a privilege to manufacture or sell liquor, despite the absence of a fundamental right to conduct that trade.
material_facts: The State exercised its exclusive regulatory privilege by granting licences to manufacture and supply liquor.
The licence applicants challenged the way the State selected recipients of those licences.
issues.conclusion: The State cannot grant liquor licences arbitrarily; its action remains subject to Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: There is no fundamental right to carry on trade or business in liquor, and the State may prohibit activities involving intoxicants. But when it grants a liquor-related right or privilege, it must comply with Article 14. The Court relied on Har Shankar v. Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner.

predicates.state_grants_liquor_privilege: The State grants a person or entity a privilege to manufacture, supply, or sell liquor.
predicates.public_licensing_action_case: The proceeding challenges public-authority action in granting a licence.

issues.definition: When a public licensing proceeding concerns a liquor privilege granted by the State, the licensing action is subject to the equality guarantee.

issues.legal_issue: A liquor-licensing policy based on considered economic and public-interest grounds does not violate equality merely because licences were initially granted to existing contractors, where similar applications remain open to consideration.
material_facts: Existing distilleries were outdated, their output was inadequate for demand, and their locations caused pollution and health concerns.
The government considered the proposal through committees, inspections, and interdepartmental review before adopting the policy.
The existing contractors offered to finance and construct modern distilleries at new sites, and the policy allowed other liquor contractors to apply on similar terms.
The State selected a private-sector arrangement to avoid public expenditure and facilitate construction before the existing licences expired.
issues.conclusion: The policy was not shown to be arbitrary, irrational, or mala fide and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 governs liquor-licensing decisions, but courts allow the State latitude in regulating an inherently pernicious trade and in making economic-policy choices. A policy may be invalidated if plainly arbitrary, irrational, discriminatory, or mala fide; a court does not substitute its preferred policy merely because another choice might seem wiser. The State is not invariably required to advertise and invite competing offers when negotiating with an enterprise proposing to establish an industry. The Court relied on R.K. Garg v. Union of India and followed Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir.

rule.if: liquor_policy_challenge_case and considered_public_interest_basis and applicants_offer_addresses_identified_need and comparable_applications_remain_open and not evidence_of_arbitrary_or_bad_faith_selection

predicates.liquor_policy_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges a government policy for granting licences connected with the manufacture or supply of liquor.
predicates.considered_public_interest_basis: The government examines relevant public needs and policy considerations through a reasoned decision-making process.
predicates.applicants_offer_addresses_identified_ne: The selected applicants offer to undertake work that addresses an identified public or economic need.
predicates.comparable_applications_remain_open: The policy permits other similarly situated applicants to seek comparable licences on comparable terms.
predicates.evidence_of_arbitrary_or_bad_faith_selec: The record contains evidence that the selection was arbitrary, irrational, discriminatory, or made in bad faith.

issues.definition: When a liquor-policy challenge involves a considered public-interest basis, an offer addressing the identified need, and an open route for comparable applications, the policy does not violate equality absent evidence of arbitrary or bad-faith selection.

issues.legal_issue: A licence to construct a distillery may be granted without a prescribed licence form or additional rules where the governing statute authorizes it and the rules permit the selected disposal method.
material_facts: The statute authorized the Excise Commissioner to license the construction and working of a distillery.
The rules did not prescribe a form for a construction licence.
The State issued letters of intent under a policy adopted by the Cabinet, using a disposal method permitted by the rules.
issues.conclusion: The policy could be implemented without making a new licence form or additional rules.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(c) of the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act authorizes licensing the construction and working of a distillery. The absence of a prescribed form does not prevent a licence from being granted. Rule XXII permits disposal in another manner directed by the State Government, and the Court relied on State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal and L.G. Chaudhari v. Secretary, Local Self Government Department, Government of Bihar.

rule.if: distillery_construction_licence_case and statute_authorizes_construction_licence and no_form_is_prescribed and rule_allows_other_disposal_method and government_adopts_that_method

predicates.distillery_construction_licence_case: The proceeding concerns a licence to construct and work a distillery.
predicates.statute_authorizes_construction_licence: The governing statute empowers the authority to license construction and operation of the facility.
predicates.no_form_is_prescribed: The applicable rules do not prescribe a particular form for the construction licence.
predicates.rule_allows_other_disposal_method: The governing rule permits disposal by another method directed by the government.
predicates.government_adopts_that_method: The government adopts a method of disposal under its policy decision.

issues.definition: When a statute authorizes a construction licence, no form is prescribed, and the government adopts a disposal method the rules permit, the licence may be granted without new rules.

issues.legal_issue: A new statutory ground that was not pleaded or supported by necessary facts in the writ proceedings cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: A party argued in the Supreme Court that the distillery operators needed a central industrial licence.
The writ petitions had not raised that ground or pleaded the facts necessary to establish its application.
The record did not show that the new distilleries would employ the number of workers that triggered the asserted licensing requirement.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not permit the new ground to be raised in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A party cannot raise for the first time in an appeal under Article 136 a factual and statutory ground that was not pleaded below and for which the necessary supporting facts are absent. Sections 3(c), 3(d), and 11 of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 made the asserted licensing requirement dependent on the relevant undertaking and workforce threshold.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_case: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.new_statutory_ground_not_pleaded_below: A party raises a statutory ground on appeal that was not raised in the proceedings below.
predicates.supporting_facts_absent: The pleadings and record do not contain the facts necessary to establish the new ground.

issues.definition: When an appeal by special leave presents an unpleaded statutory ground without supporting facts, the court will not consider that ground.

issues.legal_issue: Judges should not make harsh, disparaging findings of misconduct without adequate pleadings and evidentiary support.
material_facts: A judge made strong remarks attributing bad faith, corruption, and improper dealings to the government.
The pleadings did not give adequate particulars or identify the material facts supporting those accusations.
The record did not substantiate the accusations.
issues.conclusion: The remarks were unjustified and unwarranted and should not have been made.
issues.legal_principle: Judges should exercise sobriety, moderation, and restraint when criticizing parties or witnesses. Allegations of misconduct require adequate particulars and material facts, and unsupported disparaging remarks risk causing injustice.

predicates.judicial_opinion_case: The proceeding involves a judge's written or oral assessment of a party's conduct.
predicates.judge_makes_disparaging_misconduct_findi: The judge makes strongly disparaging remarks accusing a party of misconduct.
predicates.pleadings_or_record_support_finding: The pleadings or evidentiary record provide adequate particulars and support for the misconduct finding.

issues.definition: When a judge makes disparaging accusations in an opinion without support in the pleadings or record, the remarks are unjustified.
